title: News of Rukmini's Swayamvara
subtitle: Spies bring word from Kundina, and Krishna sets out with the Yadava host.
story:
The spies came to the house of Balarama and found there what they had hoped to find: all the leading Yadavas, gathered in assembly at Krishna's word, in a house that stood like the home of a patriarch. They had come to sow the topic of future events, and they found the whole clan ready to hear them.

What they carried was news that would set the kings of the earth in motion. At the call of the king of the Bhoja line, a great meeting of kings was to be held at the city of Kundina, and rulers from every province were already hurrying there. The word passing from mouth to mouth was this: Rukmini, the sister of Rukmi, would hold her swayamvara. Adorned with golden ornaments, the fairest woman in the three worlds, she would choose a husband on the third day from that day.

The emissaries did not spare the Yadavas the scale of the gathering, and their words carried an edge of prophecy: this meeting of kings, they announced, would be the future destruction of those same kings. The rulers were coming on elephants, horses and cars, elated with pride like lions and tigers, bent on injuring one another, gifted with the gait of infuriated elephants, fond of battle and highly powerful. The plain before Kundina would soon hold hundreds of their encampments, and the kings who feared the Yadavas would sit there in safety like immortals in the land of the celestials, under the protection of numbers.

"The kings of all the earth are assembling," they said. "Why should we remain depressed alone? Let us all, encircled by our armies, set out for victory."

The verses say the words struck Krishna like a dart to the heart. He did not deliberate long. He set out immediately at the head of his army, and the Yadavas of fierce prowess mounted their cars and followed him like the gods in their pride. Krishna shone at the head of that host, his discus and mace uplifted, he whom even Ishana held dear; and the car-warriors behind him made his beauty greater still, a stream of cars effulgent like the sun and echoing with the tinkling of bells.

But before he left, he stopped to give counsel to Ugrasena, the king. "Wait here with my brother," he said. "When this city is emptied by our departure, those kings of deceitful conduct who fear us but enjoy themselves in Kundina may attack it at Jarasandha's desire. The city must not be left unguarded."

Hearing this, the old king replied in words that trembled with affection. "O Krishna, if you go and leave us behind, we shall not be able to live here happily, or anywhere else — like a woman without her husband. Under the shelter of your arms we do not fear even Indra and the gods, much less the kings of the earth. We shall follow you wherever you go for the sake of victory."

And Krishna, hearing the king's words, smiled. "I should do whatever you wish," he said. "There is no doubt about it."

So the departure became a shared journey — the old king refusing to be left behind, and Krishna, who had begun by guarding the city, yielding to the affection of his people. The army moved out of Mathura, car after car falling into line with banners streaming until the whole might of the Yadava clan was on the road behind him, and the way to Kundina lay open before them, where the fairest woman in the three worlds was waiting to choose.
reflection: The verses say the news struck Krishna like a dart to the heart, and they do not explain why — the restraint is part of the art, as though something more than politics had been touched. The scene is doubled by Ugrasena's refusal to be left behind: the old king's devotion answers Krishna's care for the city, and a planned departure becomes a journey they take together.
next_story_tease: Krishna reached Kundina as the sun was turning red, and the assembled kings saw who had come.
hero_scene: Krishna setting out from Mathura at the head of the Yadava host, discus and mace uplifted, the army streaming behind him in sun-bright cars, while the aged king Ugrasena follows — refusing to be left behind.
visual_elements: Krishna with uplifted discus and mace
the Yadava army on cars, elephants and horses
the old king Ugrasena refusing to stay behind
a mood of resolve and departure
